records.subject: Inside Outlier: How to make a prompt yours (and read the clues)
records.body_text:
TL;DR

This week's tip: How to read a response for clues and make a prompt your own. Explore Advanced Prompt Engineering →
Your answers: How you spent Halloween. Read the thread →
Hit reply: What did you finish recently that you're proud of? Share your answer →
Hey, it's Eliana.

I spent all day yesterday working on my first quilt, and I've almost finished it. Before you get too impressed, I used precut squares, which my grandma informed me is cheating. Fair enough. Starting with precut pieces definitely gave me a head start.

Prompting works the exact same way: you don't always have to start from a blank page. Grabbing a prompt someone else started as inspiration is a great shortcut, as long as you know how to read what the model gives back and tweak the prompt until it's truly yours.

Start with inspo, then use each response to make it yours
A prompt is the question or instruction you give an AI model, and the response is what it writes back. In many Outlier tasks, you'll either write a prompt or rate how well the AI answered one.

In our course Advanced Prompt Engineering, the more advanced skill goes beyond simple right-or-wrong grading. Whether you're writing from scratch or adapting a prompt you found for inspiration, the trick is figuring out why the AI answered the way it did, and using those clues to improve your next version.

Read each response as a signal, not just an answer. If a response hedges with lots of "it depends" and "might," the model may be uncertain or missing knowledge. A response that oversimplifies can mean the prompt didn't give the model enough context. Confident errors often show up in subjects where the model has seen a lot of plausible-sounding but unreliable sources.
Treat your prompt like a rough draft. After you send a prompt, the AI's first response is a starting point, not the final word. If that response is bland, add a few more details or rules to your prompt and send it again, so you can see what the model does with a harder version. If the response misses the mark, reread your wording and look for what in your prompt might have steered the AI that way. Then rewrite the prompt and try again. Prompt revision is part of the skill.
Use your domain knowledge. Models are generalists, so they know a little about everything and less about any one field. If you're a linguist, a lawyer, a software engineer, or a medical professional, you can write prompts in your area of expertise that the model can't handle well, and spotting that gap makes your evaluation valuable.
Explore the full Advanced Prompt Engineering course →

Costumes and quiet nights: what you shared


Photo submitted by Bryan S.

Last week, I asked about your Halloween costumes, and some of you shared how you spent the night instead. Here are a few of your answers:

Holly T. took their two dogs to a dog park's "Bark-o-ween." The Great Dane went as a dragon and the mixed breed went as a dinosaur. They took home third place in the costume contest.
Katie S. made an ostrich costume out of a black trash bag, poking one arm through a hole to mimic the bird's head and neck. The friends who were supposed to match never showed up, and Katie says there were "more laughs" that way.
Mohammed B. dressed up as "a complex prompt with conflicting constraints" and walked around telling people things that sounded confident and coherent but were completely made up.
